title: An address moved to a different machine

chain.why: This address is now answered by hardware that was not previously bound to it, so the machine behind it is a different machine.

advice: Normal after a DHCP lease expires. Worth a look if the address is a server, is statically assigned, or moved without a lease renewal near it.

title: The default gateway is being answered by a different machine

chain.why: The hardware address answering for the default gateway changed. Every host on this segment now sends its outbound traffic to a different machine.

evidence.describe: 10.99.0.201 moved from 02:00:00:00:00:01 to 02:00:00:00:00:ff - this is the default gateway

chain.subject: default
chain.why: Routing followed the change, so traffic is now leaving through a path nobody chose.

evidence.describe: the default route now goes via 10.99.0.202 (was 10.99.0.201)

chain.why: Connectivity was lost while the gateway was being answered elsewhere.

advice: Find which switch port the new hardware address is learned on before changing anything. A failover looks identical to an attack from here; the port tells them apart.

title: Two machines are claiming the same address

chain.why: The hardware address answering for this address kept changing between the same few machines, which is what an address conflict looks like from the neighbour table.

evidence.describe: 10.99.0.11 is being claimed by more than one machine

chain.why: The address stopped answering reliably while it was contested.

advice: Check for a statically configured host inside the DHCP pool, or a second DHCP server. Both produce this, and both keep producing it until one is removed.

title: The default route was re-pointed

chain.subject: default
chain.why: The route all outbound traffic follows now points somewhere else.

evidence.describe: the default route now goes via 10.99.0.202 (was 10.99.0.201)

chain.subject: default
chain.why: Reachability changed once the traffic started taking the new path.

evidence.describe: the default route was removed - nothing beyond the local segment is reachable

advice: Confirm this was intended. Compare the time against your change record: an unplanned default route change means outbound traffic is leaving through a path nobody chose.

title: The default route disappeared

chain.subject: default
chain.why: The default route was withdrawn. Nothing beyond the local segment is reachable from here.

evidence.describe: the default route was removed - nothing beyond the local segment is reachable

chain.why: Reachability began failing once there was no default path.

advice: Look at the timeline immediately before this. A default route rarely leaves on its own; it follows an interface going down, a DHCP lease expiring, or a routing daemon losing its peer. Fix that, not the route.

title: A service stopped answering

chain.why: Repeated connections to this service went from the opening SYN straight to closed without ever being answered. Something refused them, dropped them, or was not listening.

advice: Check whether the service is listening before blaming the network. If it is, look at the timeline for a filtering change or a route change just before the first failure - both look identical from the client.

title: A measured path stopped answering

chain.why: This is the last thing that changed before the path stopped answering.
Probes to this address began going unanswered. Packet loss announces itself to nobody; it has to be measured, and it was.
It later answered again, which bounds how long the outage lasted.

advice: This is measured, not reported: the recorder sent probes and they did not come back. If the change named above was intended, the loss is a side effect nobody planned. If there is no change above it, the fault is beyond what this recorder can see from where it sits.

title: A path that was working stopped working

chain.why: This is the last thing that changed on the path before it broke.
Two machines that had been connecting successfully can no longer complete a handshake. Whatever else is true, something between them changed.

evidence.describe: 10.99.1.1 can no longer reach 10.99.1.11 on port 9200 - it worked 5s ago

chain.why: Other connections started failing in the same window.

advice: The change named here is the nearest one in time, not a proven cause. Confirm it against your change record before acting: if it was intended, the breakage is a side effect nobody planned; if it was not, something changed the network without going through you.

title: A link went down and took hosts with it

chain.subject: nrlab1
chain.why: An interface went down.
Hosts stopped answering at layer 2 immediately afterwards, which is the link failure showing up as apparent host failures.

advice: The hosts did not fail. Restore the link and they will return; investigating them individually wastes the outage.

title: A second DHCP server is answering on this segment

chain.why: A DHCP server answered on a segment that already had one. Every client that renews from here on gets whichever of them replies first.

evidence.describe: a second DHCP server appeared on 10.99.0.99, handing out 10.99.0.99 as the gateway

chain.why: Clients began taking different addresses, gateways or resolvers, which is the second server's configuration arriving.

advice: Find the switch port the new server's hardware address is learned on and shut it. Almost always a consumer router plugged in the wrong way round, with its LAN side facing the network. Until it is off, clients will keep taking its addresses and its gateway at random.

title: A machine's resolver changed under it

chain.why: This is what changed on the path just before the resolver did.
This machine started sending its lookups somewhere else. Every name it resolves from here on is answered by a different party.

advice: Compare against your DHCP scope. A client that changed resolver without a lease renewal near it did not choose to; something told it to. Check for a second DHCP server and for the gateway's hardware address changing at about the same time.

title: A port is flapping

chain.subject: nrlab0
chain.why: The same interface went down repeatedly in a few minutes. One outage is an event; a run of them is a fault in the link itself.

chain.subject: nrlab0
chain.why: It came back each time, which is why nobody noticed it was failing.

advice: A port that flaps repeatedly is usually a failing transceiver, a marginal cable, or a duplex mismatch. Restarting the interface will not fix any of those, and hides the evidence.
